title: Knowledge Check 4: Lessons 16-20
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 16-20 of the hermes-consultant-advanced series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A high-potential operator two years from principal is already performing well. Which relationship do they actually need?
options: More management, because objectives and role performance are still unproven.
Coaching on how to work faster within the current role.
Mentoring on judgment and sponsorship into the room where the client relationship and the numbers live.
All four relationships at once, so nothing is missed.
questions.explanation: A high performer needs the relationships that expand capability: mentoring on judgment and sponsorship into rooms where development can happen.

questions.question: What actually transfers delivery judgment from a principal to an operator?
options: Handing the operator the written standard to read until it is memorized.
Letting the operator shadow the principal for a full year before deciding.
Reviewing the operator's output against the acceptance criteria after each delivery.
A progression of observation, then committed decisions compared against the principal's, then earned autonomy, then independent judgment.
questions.explanation: Judgment transfers when the operator commits to a decision and sees the delta against the mentor's reasoning, not by being told the answer.

questions.question: What distinguishes senior delivery talent from a mid-level operator?
options: The ability to author the standard: write the criteria, place the gate, review others, and own the estimate.
More years of experience across a wider range of clients.
A higher utilization rate on client-billable work.
The habit of escalating fewer problems over time.
questions.explanation: The step up is owning the framework, authoring the standard and review, not just performing well inside it.

questions.question: What is the real measure that a consulting practice has scaled?
options: Growing headcount until the team can carry more concurrent client engagements.
How much the practice's annual revenue has grown over the prior year.
Whether deliverables still meet the bar when the principal is unavailable.
How many named clients the practice has signed across all its segments.
questions.explanation: Scaling is defined by how much work the practice can deliver without the principal's judgment in the path, not by headcount or revenue.

questions.question: Why must the separation of the author from the reviewer come before the other separations?
options: Because clients expect a written review process before they sign any work.
Because a second seller cannot be brought on until the pricing model is fully built.
Because without a review gate, more deliverers only add unsupervised output.
Because the principal must stop billing hours before any other capacity can be added.
questions.explanation: A review gate against a written standard is what makes good work repeatable; without it, more deliverers multiply unsupervised output rather than real capacity.

questions.question: A principal must choose between a quarter that personally bills a large engagement and a quarter spent building a new lead and a new service line. How should the two be compared?
options: On revenue, because the personally billed work funds later development.
On the principal's own utilization, because that measures the scarce resource.
On client satisfaction, because a strong reputation drives future referrals.
On which option increases the work the firm can carry without the principal.
questions.explanation: The right comparison is which option moves the firm further toward running without the founder, since revenue can grow while the practice stays dependent on one person.

questions.question: Why model a practice's finances at the unit level instead of in annual totals?
options: Because annual totals hide the fixed costs that unit modeling exposes.
Because lenders require unit economics before they will extend credit.
Because annual profit is too volatile and unpredictable to model at all.
Because the unit is where price, cost, and volume can be acted on.
questions.explanation: Unit-level numbers expose the price, cost, and volume levers a principal can actually act on; aggregate totals collapse them together.

questions.question: Two practices show the same healthy per-unit contribution but different runway. What does the runway difference determine?
options: Which one can afford to spend a quarter on non-delivery work.
Which one has the higher contribution per unit on its offers.
Which one has the lower variable delivery cost per unit.
Which one can raise prices without losing any existing clients.
questions.explanation: Runway is the budget that makes an investment available; a thin runway forces survival decisions while a long one lets the firm absorb a quarter without revenue.

questions.question: A practice shows strong contribution on every unit but a negative practice margin. What does that reveal?
options: That the flagship offer is underpriced relative to the value it delivers.
That the fixed-cost base is too heavy for the volume of units sold.
That the delivery cost of each unit is higher than the market rate.
That the practice's runway must be longer than twelve months to be safe.
questions.explanation: Unit contribution pays the fixed base; when contribution is healthy but practice margin is negative, the fixed base is too large for the volume of units sold.

questions.question: What distinguishes a true client partnership from a vendor relationship?
options: The client renews the contract without renegotiating its terms each cycle.
The client reports strong satisfaction in an annual relationship review.
The client pays a recurring fee each month rather than per project.
The client raises problems early and consults before they become urgent.
questions.explanation: Satisfaction and renewal can both happen without commitment; a partner is given early access to problems and roadmap, the raw material that can only be earned.

questions.question: Why is retention the single biggest lever on a recurring revenue business?
options: Because a retained dollar keeps paying, while a new one must be won.
Because retained clients always agree to pay a higher monthly fee.
Because retention removes all variable delivery cost from an account.
Because high retention lets a practice stop measuring its margins.
questions.explanation: A retained client keeps paying at a lower retention cost, so improving retention compounds, while each new client must be won again from zero.

questions.question: A recurring account's invoice stays flat while the cost of delivering it creeps up. Which risk does that describe?
options: Concentration risk from a single anchor client dominating the base.
The vendor trap, where a partnership quietly decays into a low-touch subscription.
Margin drift, where a deliverable's margin erodes while the invoice holds.
Value drift, where a fee tied to an outcome stops matching the result.
questions.explanation: Margin drift is silent because the invoice holds steady while rising delivery cost erodes the margin, which is why accounts are measured on a margin cadence.

questions.question: Why is excellent delivery not enough on its own to bring work in the door?
options: Because buyers judge the promise of delivery before they can evaluate it.
Because strong delivery tends to make a team complacent about its own quality.
Because referrals stop arriving once a practice leaves hourly billing behind.
Because buyers insist on evaluating delivery before agreeing to any first call.
questions.explanation: A buyer purchases the promise of delivery as it is represented in positioning, offer, and proof, so excellent work stays invisible without a plan to present it.

questions.question: What test separates a real go-to-market plan from an aspiration?
options: Whether an advisor outside the practice has approved the document.
Whether every section names a revenue target and a deadline for it.
Whether the document lists both inbound and outbound marketing motions.
Whether a competent stranger could run the document for a quarter.
questions.explanation: A plan is executable by someone other than its author; a section a competent stranger cannot run is a resolution, not a decision.

questions.question: A go-to-market plan is built from decisions, not aspirations. What makes a section a decision?
options: It names the marketing software the practice will run the plan on.
It commits to a choice that closes off a real alternative.
It sets a quarterly revenue target the whole team is accountable to.
It selects the single competitor the practice will position against.
questions.explanation: Every part of the plan is a commitment that closes off alternatives, which is what lets someone other than the author execute it.
